questions.questionText: Which inference is best supported by the visual clues?
options: A gust through the window scattered the papers
A student deliberately sorted the papers
The classroom was locked all day
Rain soaked every sheet of paper
questions.correctAnswer: A gust through the window scattered the papers
questions.explanation: The open window, moving curtain and scattered papers together support the gust inference.

curriculum.objective: Select and connect explicit and implicit evidence to explain inference, viewpoint and theme.

questions.questionText: “Amir reread the message, typed a reply, deleted it, and placed the phone face down.” What can be inferred?
options: He cannot read the message
He is uncertain how to respond
His phone battery is empty
He has already sent several replies
questions.correctAnswer: He is uncertain how to respond
questions.explanation: Drafting and deleting a reply before hiding the screen suggests hesitation or uncertainty.

curriculum.objective: Select and connect explicit and implicit evidence to explain inference, viewpoint and theme.

questions.questionText: Which detail most strongly shows that the narrator distrusts the guide?
options: The guide carries a red bag
The group walks before lunch
The narrator checks every direction against an old map
The path contains small stones
questions.correctAnswer: The narrator checks every direction against an old map
questions.explanation: Checking each direction independently is purposeful evidence that the narrator doubts the guide.

curriculum.objective: Select and connect explicit and implicit evidence to explain inference, viewpoint and theme.

questions.questionText: A story repeatedly contrasts a locked gate with birds flying overhead. Which theme is most strongly suggested?
options: The value of expensive objects
The difficulty of learning bird names
The importance of matching colours
The desire for freedom
questions.correctAnswer: The desire for freedom
questions.explanation: The contrast between confinement and free flight develops a theme about longing for freedom.

curriculum.objective: Select and connect explicit and implicit evidence to explain inference, viewpoint and theme.

questions.questionText: What effect does “stitched a path through the storm” create?
options: It presents the light as joining darkness into a safe route
It states that the lighthouse repairs clothing
It proves the storm has completely ended
It gives the exact distance to the shore
questions.correctAnswer: It presents the light as joining darkness into a safe route
questions.explanation: The metaphor makes the beam seem to join a visible route through dangerous darkness.

curriculum.objective: Analyse how figurative language, imagery and precise vocabulary shape meaning and reader response.

questions.questionText: In “The deadline crept closer,” what is personified?
options: The writer
The deadline
The clock face
The completed task
questions.correctAnswer: The deadline
questions.explanation: The abstract deadline is given the living action of creeping closer.

curriculum.objective: Analyse how figurative language, imagery and precise vocabulary shape meaning and reader response.

questions.questionText: Which verb most strongly suggests a door closed with sudden force?
options: Moved
Rested
Slammed
Opened with slow and deliberate care
questions.correctAnswer: Slammed
questions.explanation: Slammed precisely conveys both rapid movement and forceful impact.

curriculum.objective: Analyse how figurative language, imagery and precise vocabulary shape meaning and reader response.

questions.questionText: Why might a writer describe silence as “heavy” after an argument?
options: To measure the mass of the room
To show that everyone became louder
To explain the furniture arrangement
To suggest tension that feels difficult to bear
questions.correctAnswer: To suggest tension that feels difficult to bear
questions.explanation: The sensory metaphor turns emotional tension into something that seems physically burdensome.

curriculum.objective: Analyse how figurative language, imagery and precise vocabulary shape meaning and reader response.

questions.questionText: Which option correctly uses a semicolon to connect two complete clauses?
options: The storm had passed; the roads were still flooded.
The storm; had passed the roads were still flooded.
The storm had; passed, the roads were still flooded.
The storm had passed the; roads were still flooded.
questions.correctAnswer: The storm had passed; the roads were still flooded.
questions.explanation: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.

curriculum.objective: Control clauses, punctuation, reference and tense to create accurate, cohesive sentences.

questions.questionText: Choose the sentence with consistent tense.
options: Mina opens the gate and walked into the garden.
Mina opened the gate and walked into the garden.
Mina had opened the gate and walks inside.
Mina opening the gate and walked inside.
questions.correctAnswer: Mina opened the gate and walked into the garden.
questions.explanation: Both verbs are in the simple past, so the sequence is grammatically consistent.

curriculum.objective: Control clauses, punctuation, reference and tense to create accurate, cohesive sentences.

questions.questionText: Which revision makes the pronoun reference clear?
options: When Daria met Leila, she carried it.
She met her while carrying it.
When Daria met Leila, Daria carried the portfolio.
When they met, she carried the portfolio.
questions.correctAnswer: When Daria met Leila, Daria carried the portfolio.
questions.explanation: Repeating Daria removes ambiguity about which person carried the portfolio.

curriculum.objective: Control clauses, punctuation, reference and tense to create accurate, cohesive sentences.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly punctuates a non-essential clause?
options: The library which opened, in 1920 is being restored.
The library which, opened in 1920 is being restored.
The library which opened in 1920, is being restored.
The library, which opened in 1920, is being restored.
questions.correctAnswer: The library, which opened in 1920, is being restored.
questions.explanation: The removable relative clause is enclosed by a matching pair of commas.

curriculum.objective: Control clauses, punctuation, reference and tense to create accurate, cohesive sentences.

questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of the explanation box in the article plan?
options: To show how the evidence supports the central idea
To introduce an unrelated topic
To repeat the headline word for word
To list sources without discussing them
questions.correctAnswer: To show how the evidence supports the central idea
questions.explanation: Explanation connects selected evidence to the central idea so the reasoning is clear.

curriculum.objective: Organise claims, evidence and explanations into coherent texts with purposeful transitions and conclusions.

questions.questionText: Which transition best introduces a consequence?
options: In contrast
As a result
For instance
Meanwhile
questions.correctAnswer: As a result
questions.explanation: As a result explicitly signals that the next idea is a consequence of the previous one.

curriculum.objective: Organise claims, evidence and explanations into coherent texts with purposeful transitions and conclusions.

questions.questionText: Which evidence best supports the claim that a reading club increased participation?
options: The club poster uses bright colours
One member likes adventure stories
Attendance records rose from 18 to 31 students over six weeks
The library has four windows
questions.correctAnswer: Attendance records rose from 18 to 31 students over six weeks
questions.explanation: Comparable attendance data directly measures the claimed change in participation.

curriculum.objective: Organise claims, evidence and explanations into coherent texts with purposeful transitions and conclusions.

questions.questionText: Which conclusion most effectively closes an argument for safer crossings near school?
options: That is everything I know about roads.
Crossings can be painted in several colours.
My first paragraph already explained the problem.
Installing marked crossings would address the documented risk and protect all road users.
questions.correctAnswer: Installing marked crossings would address the documented risk and protect all road users.
questions.explanation: The sentence returns to the evidence-based claim and states its wider significance.

curriculum.objective: Organise claims, evidence and explanations into coherent texts with purposeful transitions and conclusions.

questions.questionText: Who is the campaign poster most directly trying to persuade?
options: Students who can choose reusable bottles
Engineers designing water pipes
Historians studying old containers in museums
Pilots planning a flight route
questions.correctAnswer: Students who can choose reusable bottles
questions.explanation: The school-style slogan, bottle symbol and scan-to-join action target student choices.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate how tone, design and persuasive choices suit audience, purpose and communication medium.

questions.questionText: Which opening best suits a formal report to the school board?
options: Hey everyone, here is what we reckon!
This report evaluates three options using cost, safety and access data.
Once upon a time there were three options.
You will never believe option two!
questions.correctAnswer: This report evaluates three options using cost, safety and access data.
questions.explanation: The opening states purpose and criteria in a neutral, appropriately formal tone.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate how tone, design and persuasive choices suit audience, purpose and communication medium.

questions.questionText: A headline says “Miracle Study Trick Guarantees Success!” What should a careful reader check first?
options: Whether the headline uses a capital letter
Whether the page background is blue
Whether credible evidence supports the absolute claim
Whether the article contains a photograph
questions.correctAnswer: Whether credible evidence supports the absolute claim
questions.explanation: The guarantee is an extreme claim, so source quality and supporting evidence require scrutiny.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate how tone, design and persuasive choices suit audience, purpose and communication medium.

questions.questionText: Which change most improves an emergency notice for a multilingual audience?
options: Add dense paragraphs of unfamiliar technical slang and abbreviations
Use colour as the only warning signal
Replace instructions with a humorous story
Use short steps, clear symbols and tested translations
questions.correctAnswer: Use short steps, clear symbols and tested translations
questions.explanation: Concise steps, redundant symbols and verified translations improve speed, clarity and access.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate how tone, design and persuasive choices suit audience, purpose and communication medium.
